hints: Think about the path of the signal - where does the signal go after it leaves the output of the op-amp in a circuit with feedback?
Focus on what is being transferred back and combined - it is an electrical quantity from the output added to the original input.
walkthrough:
**Picture what feedback means**
Imagine the amplifier as a loop rather than a one-way street. Normally a signal goes in and a bigger signal comes out. With feedback, you take a little sample of what comes out and feed it back round to join what goes in.

**Write the precise definition**
So you can say it simply as: part of the output is combined with the input. To get full credit, name the quantity involved, so say output potential difference, voltage or signal is fed back and combined with the input potential, voltage or signal.
Final answer: Feedback is when a fraction of the output voltage/signal is combined with the input voltage/signal.

hints: Think about why an op-amp with huge open-loop gain is hard to control, and what happens to the gain value when you apply negative feedback.
Think about the quality of the amplified sound or signal - what happens to distortion and to the range of frequencies that are amplified evenly?
walkthrough:
**Why tame the gain**
An ideal op-amp on its own has enormous gain that drifts with temperature and supply changes. Negative feedback sacrifices some of that huge gain to make the closed-loop gain depend only on resistors, so you get much greater operating stability.

**Better fidelity**
The same trade gives two other classic benefits. The amplifier works evenly over a larger bandwidth, meaning a wider range of frequencies is amplified by the same amount, and any distortion of the output waveform is reduced, so the output is a cleaner copy of the input.
Final answer: Any two from: increased operating stability of gain, increased bandwidth / wider range of frequencies with constant gain, reduced distortion of output.

hints: Start with the measured values for this circuit - what is the input voltage at point P and the corresponding output voltage V_OUT?
Recall how overall voltage gain links those two voltages for any amplifier.
Look at Fig. 7.1 and identify the type of op-amp circuit and which resistor is the feedback resistor between output and the inverting input.
Use the resistor gain formula to link your gain value to the 92.5 kΩ resistor and unknown R, then rearrange for R and check units.
walkthrough:
**Find the gain from voltages**
For any voltage amplifier the gain is simply output divided by input: $$G = \frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}}$$ Here $V_{IN}$ is the potential at P, $48 \text{ mV} = 48 \times 10^{-3} \text{ V}$, and $V_{OUT} = 3.6 \text{ V}$. So $$G = \frac{3.6}{48 \times 10^{-3}} = 75$$ Gain has no unit.

**Recognise the non-inverting amplifier**
In Fig. 7.1 the microphone signal goes to the + input, and a divider of $92.5 \text{ k}\Omega$ and $R$ feeds back to the - input. That is a non-inverting amplifier, for which $$G = 1 + \frac{R_F}{R}$$ where $R_F = 92.5 \times 10^{3} \ \Omega$ is the feedback resistor.

**Solve for R**
Put the numbers in: $$75 = 1 + \frac{92.5 \times 10^{3}}{R}$$ so $$74 = \frac{92.5 \times 10^{3}}{R}$$ $$R = \frac{92.5 \times 10^{3}}{74} \approx 1.25 \times 10^{3} \ \Omega \approx 1.3 \times 10^{3} \ \Omega$$ About $1300 \ \Omega$.
Final answer: Gain $= V_{OUT}/V_{IN} = 3.6/(48 \times 10^{-3}) = 75$. For non-inverting amplifier, $G = 1 + R_F/R$, so $75 = 1 + (92.5 \times 10^{3})/R$ giving $R = 1.3 \times 10^{3} \ \Omega$.

hints: Calculate what the ideal output would be for 68 mV input using the gain of 75 you just found, and compare it with the op-amp supply voltages of +5.0 V and -5.0 V.
Recall what happens when the calculated output tries to go beyond what the power supply can provide.
walkthrough:
**Test the ideal output**
With $G = 75$, an input of $68 \text{ mV}$ would ideally give: $$V_{OUT} = G \times V_{IN} = 75 \times 68 \times 10^{-3} \approx 5.1 \text{ V}$$

**Apply the supply limit**
But the op-amp is powered from +5.0 V and -5.0 V, so the output can never exceed about the supply voltage. Since 5.1 V is greater than +5.0 V, the amplifier saturates and the output sticks at about 5.0 V, clipping the top of the waveform.
Final answer: Ideal output $= 75 \times 68 \times 10^{-3} = 5.1 \text{ V}$ which exceeds the +5.0 V supply, so the op-amp saturates and $V_{OUT}$ is limited to about 5.0 V.
